subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for recurrent abdominal pain. He is thin for his age with poor hygiene, unkempt clothing, and a withdrawn affect. His height and weight have fallen off the growth curve over the past year. The parents report frequent household instability but there is no history of witnessed trauma or unexplained injuries.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the form of maltreatment this child is most likely experiencing?

options.text: Nonaccidental trauma with injuries in different stages of healing
Failure to provide adequate food, shelter, supervision, education, or affection
Involuntary obscene speech and repetitive motor tics
Sexual knowledge or behavior incongruent with the child's age
Overly affectionate behavior toward unfamiliar adults with aggression toward animals

explanation_correct: This child shows poor hygiene, malnutrition, withdrawn affect, and failure to thrive — the classic signs of neglect, which results from failure to provide adequate food, shelter, supervision, education, and/or affection. Neglect is the most common form of child maltreatment. All forms of suspected child abuse must be reported to local child protective services. The absence of injuries does not exclude abuse, because neglect may produce no physical findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Injuries in different stages of healing or patterned bruises/burns suggest physical abuse, not neglect; this child has no such injuries.
explanation_incorrect.C: Involuntary obscene speech (coprolalia) and motor tics characterize Tourette syndrome, not a form of maltreatment.
explanation_incorrect.D: Age-inappropriate sexual knowledge or behavior points toward sexual abuse, which typically presents differently from failure to thrive and poor hygiene.
explanation_incorrect.E: Being overly affectionate with strangers and aggressive toward animals are features of emotional abuse, not the neglect described here.

educationalObjective: Neglect is the most common form of child abuse and presents with failure to thrive, poor hygiene, and withdrawn affect from failure to provide basic needs.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 7-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department lethargic after a witnessed collapse. Imaging reveals a subdural hematoma, and fundoscopic examination shows retinal hemorrhages. The caregiver's explanation of the injury is inconsistent with the infant's developmental abilities. There are no external signs of trauma.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and the required next step in management?

options.text: Neglect; arrange nutritional support and social work follow-up only
Sexual abuse; perform a sexual assault examination and report to law enforcement
Abusive head trauma; report the case to child protective services
Emotional abuse; begin play therapy and monitor the caregiver-child bond
Benign accidental injury; discharge with reassurance and routine follow-up

explanation_correct: Subdural hematoma with retinal hemorrhages in an infant is the classic presentation of abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome), a form of physical abuse. Caregiver explanations inconsistent with the child's developmental stage further support nonaccidental trauma. All cases of suspected child abuse must be reported to local child protective services. Approximately 40% of abuse-related deaths occur in children younger than 1 year.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neglect causes failure to thrive and poor hygiene, not subdural hematoma with retinal hemorrhage; reporting is mandatory regardless.
explanation_incorrect.B: Sexual abuse is associated with STIs, UTIs, and genital/anal/oral trauma, not this pattern of intracranial and retinal injury.
explanation_incorrect.D: Emotional abuse involves disturbed caregiver bonding and somatic complaints, not the focal traumatic findings described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: These findings are not a benign accidental injury; the pattern is highly specific for nonaccidental trauma and must be reported.

educationalObjective: Subdural hematoma plus retinal hemorrhage in an infant signals abusive head trauma, which like all suspected abuse must be reported to child protective services.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent urinary tract infections. She has a mild perineal tear, and testing identifies a sexually transmitted infection. On interview she demonstrates detailed sexual knowledge far beyond her years and describes sexual activity with an older household member. No external injuries were initially noted on brief examination.
question: Which of the following statements regarding this presentation is most accurate?

options.text: Sexual abuse must be considered even when physical signs are absent or minimal
The peak incidence of sexual abuse is in adolescence, around ages 15-17
Age-inappropriate sexual knowledge is more suggestive of emotional neglect than abuse
A normal external examination effectively excludes sexual abuse in most cases
Reporting is optional unless the caregiver is the alleged perpetrator

explanation_correct: Sexual abuse commonly presents with STIs, UTIs, and genital, anal, or oral trauma, but most often there are no physical signs; thus abuse should not be excluded when physical trauma is absent. Children frequently exhibit sexual knowledge or behavior incongruent with their age, as in this case. Peak incidence is 9-12 years old, matching this patient's age. All suspected abuse must be reported to child protective services.

explanation_incorrect.B: Peak incidence of sexual abuse is 9-12 years, not late adolescence; this patient's age is actually the peak range.
explanation_incorrect.C: Age-incongruent sexual knowledge is a hallmark of sexual abuse, not emotional neglect or another form of maltreatment.
explanation_incorrect.D: Most cases of sexual abuse have no physical signs, so a normal examination does not exclude it.
explanation_incorrect.E: All cases of suspected child abuse must be reported to child protective services regardless of who the perpetrator is.

educationalObjective: Sexual abuse often lacks physical findings and peaks at ages 9-12; age-inappropriate sexual knowledge is a key clue and reporting is mandatory.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 3-year-old is evaluated after her pediatrician notes she is unusually wary of her mother, becomes anxious in her mother's presence, and is overly affectionate toward unfamiliar clinic staff. She has difficulty calming down, is aggressive toward other children, and complains of frequent stomachaches for which no medical cause is found. There are no bruises, burns, or fractures.
question: Which form of maltreatment is most consistent with this child's presentation?

options.text: Physical abuse with nonaccidental patterned injuries
Neglect with failure to thrive and poor hygiene
Sexual abuse with age-inappropriate sexual behavior
Emotional abuse with abnormal caregiver bonding
Vulnerable child syndrome following a serious illness

explanation_correct: Lack of a bond with the caregiver, being overly affectionate with less familiar adults, aggression, unusual anxiety, emotional lability, and vague somatic symptoms without medical explanation are classic features of emotional abuse. Approximately 80% of young adult victims of child emotional abuse meet criteria for at least one psychiatric illness by age 21. Like all suspected abuse, this must be reported to child protective services.

explanation_incorrect.A: Physical abuse produces nonaccidental trauma such as fractures, bruises, or burns in various stages of healing, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neglect presents with malnutrition, poor hygiene, and failure to thrive rather than the disturbed bonding and somatic complaints seen in this child.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sexual abuse is suggested by STIs, UTIs, trauma, or age-incongruent sexual knowledge, none of which are described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vulnerable child syndrome involves parental misperception of a child as medically fragile after a serious illness, not the emotional and behavioral findings in this case.

educationalObjective: Emotional abuse presents with impaired caregiver bonding, anxiety, aggression, and medically unexplained somatic symptoms, with high rates of later psychiatric illness.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 6-year-old boy had a life-threatening pneumonia requiring prolonged hospitalization at age 2. Since discharge, his parents have repeatedly kept him home from school for minor complaints and sought numerous unnecessary medical evaluations, fearing he is especially susceptible to illness. He is otherwise developing normally and there is no evidence of intentional harm or fabricated illness.
question: Which of the following best describes this parental behavior?

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on another because the caregiver is fabricating symptoms
Emotional abuse because the parents are overly affectionate with strangers
Neglect because the child is not receiving adequate medical attention
Vulnerable child syndrome due to misperception of the child as fragile
Separation anxiety disorder because the child avoids school

explanation_correct: Vulnerable child syndrome occurs when parents misperceive a child as especially susceptible to illness or injury, usually after a serious illness or life-threatening event. It can result in missed school and overuse of medical services — the 'child wrapped in bubble wrap' — and is distinguished from factitious disorder imposed on another, in which the caregiver directly causes or fabricates illness. The parents' fears here are genuine rather than intentional fabrication.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factitious disorder imposed on another requires the caregiver to directly cause or fabricate illness in the child; here the concern is a genuine misperception, not intentional production of symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.B: Emotional abuse involves impaired bonding, anxiety, and aggression, not a misperception of medical fragility after an illness.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neglect is failure to provide adequate food, shelter, supervision, education, or affection; here the parents are overusing, not avoiding, medical care.
explanation_incorrect.E: Separation anxiety disorder is a child's overwhelming fear of separation lasting at least 4 weeks, not a parental misperception of fragility.

educationalObjective: Vulnerable child syndrome is a parental misperception of fragility after a serious childhood illness, leading to school absence and excessive medical use, and is distinct from factitious disorder imposed on another.
